P no content NECESSARY ... e assessment has no input; withdrawn≠invalidated collapses NECESSARY ... c contradicts(A1,A3) becomes true — executed false positive
a_rows_sample.statement: Component-by-component minimality/removal audit (§10), each tested by executed removal: A, R, id, P, e, c, t, and Pi are each found NECESSARY (removing any one produces a demonstrated failure — e.g. removing c makes contradicts(A1,A3) become an executed false positive, removing t loses the temporal-overlap test for contradiction, removing Pi makes origin unreconstructible at t=0); Sigma is DERIVED (recomputable from e, hence not independently necessary); History is EXTERNAL (an executed counterexample shows it does not belong inside K); Policy and Authority are EXTERNAL T-parameters; Zero (Z) and Lord Candidate (L) are REDUNDANT for the specified transformation set T because no tested operation consumes them.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The model is executable, so removal is testable. The phrase MINIMAL KERNEL is therefore earned — but only in the sense step 254 names: Minimality(K | 𝒯), relative to the transformation set. Not ontological necessity. A richer 𝒯 could force more.
a_rows_sample.statement: Minimality caveat: the removal-based necessity audit only earns Minimality(K|T) relative to the specific tested transformation set T (per step 254's framing), never ontological necessity of the components — a richer transformation set could force additional components to become necessary.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K = (𝒜, ℛ) ; 𝒜 = Set(Assertion) Assertion = (id, P, e, c, t, Π) ; P = (E, D, V) ... ℛ = ℛ_sup ⊎ ℛ_ref ⊎ ℛ_der ⊎ ℛ_supp ⊎ ℛ_res ⊎ ℛ_rel ; DAGs: sup, ref, der non-transitive: supp, res symmetric: rel ; DERIVED, never stored: Σ · equals · contradicts · conflictsWith ; EXTERNAL: History · Policy · Autho
a_rows_sample.statement: The canonical statement of the whole artifact: K=(A,R) with A a set of Assertion=(id,P,e,c,t,Pi) where P=(E,D,V), e a subset of Evidence=(ref,polarity,state), c in Context, t a half-open interval [vf,vt), Pi in Origin; R is a disjoint union of six relation kinds (supersedes, references, derived_from, supports, restricts/res, related_to) with sup/ref/der required to be DAGs, supp/res non-transitive, and rel symmetric; Sigma (epistemic status), equals, contradicts and conflictsWith are DERIVED and never stored; History, Policy, Authority, and Gamma are EXTERNAL to K.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ℛ_rel (symmetric related_to) is new — it comes from the EKP ... acyclicity must NOT be required of it — executed: the real EKP graph has a related_to cycle (KNOWLEDGE-CONSTITUTION ↔ META-LIFECYCLE), which is correct behaviour for a symmetric relation, not a defect. The theory had no symmetric relati
a_rows_sample.statement: R_rel (symmetric related_to), accounting for 46 of the EKP's 51 real edges, is a genuinely new relation family the theory had not previously included — supplied by the implementation, not derived in advance; it must NOT be required to be acyclic, and indeed the real EKP graph contains a related_to cycle (KNOWLEDGE-CONSTITUTION <-> META-LIFECYCLE) which is correct behavior for a symmetric relation, not a defect.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Hr = [assert A1, assert A4] ; Hs = [assert A4, assert A1] ... F(Hr) = F(Hs) = True ... i = relate(A1,A4,supersedes) -> congruent: True ... i = assert A2 -> congruent: True ... i = relate(A4,A1,refines) -> congruent: True ... F(H1) = F(H3) where H3 re-asserts A1 (idempotence) -> congruent: True. No c
a_rows_sample.statement: Valid executed congruence test: order-reversed histories Hr=[assert A1, assert A4] and Hs=[assert A4, assert A1] satisfy the precondition F(Hr)=F(Hs); three different subsequent operations (relate-supersedes, assert, relate-refines) are each tested and found congruent, plus an idempotence test (re-asserting A1); no counterexample is found across these tests.

a_rows_sample.anchor: T's derived signature is 𝕂 × Op × Policy × Authority ⇀ 𝕂 × Outcome. History is not in its domain. A function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. Congruence therefore holds by construction, under exactly two assumptions: A1 · T reads only K, Policy, Authority — PROVEN ... A2 · no operat
a_rows_sample.statement: Structural (by-construction) explanation for why congruence held in every test: T's derived signature K x Op x Policy x Authority -harpoon-> K x Outcome does not include History in its domain, so T cannot depend on it — a function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. This holds under exactly two assumptions: A1 (T reads only K, Policy, Authority — PROVEN by elimination of actor/time/evidence/context during signature derivation) and A2 (no operation consults order-of-arrival — HOLDS for the twelve derived operations because A and R are sets, making order structurally unobservable).

a_rows_sample.anchor: A2 is the one that could fail. Any future operation reading insertion order — "the first assertion wins", "the most recently added is authoritative" — breaks congruence immediately. That is a design constraint the theory now states explicitly rather than assumes silently.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit forward-looking design constraint: assumption A2 (no operation consults insertion order) is violable by future design — any future operation implementing 'first assertion wins' or 'most recently added is authoritative' semantics would break congruence immediately; the theory now states this as an explicit constraint rather than a silent assumption.

a_rows_sample.anchor: SUFFICIENT UNDER ASSUMPTIONS. Not sufficient unqualified: the assumptions are real and A2 is violable by future design. Not insufficient: no counterexample exists and none can, given A1. Not unknown: the test was constructed correctly and executed.
a_rows_sample.statement: Final classification: the Knowledge-State/History sufficiency question is SUFFICIENT UNDER ASSUMPTIONS — deliberately neither 'sufficient unqualified' (the assumptions A1/A2 are real and A2 is violable), nor 'insufficient' (no counterexample exists, and none can given A1), nor 'unknown' (the test was validly constructed and executed).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge State is sufficient for FUTURE COMPUTATION. It is NOT sufficient for GOVERNANCE AUDIT. ... Who asserted this, and when? NO ... Was every admission properly authorised? NO — GovernanceValid(K,Γ) needs History ... What did we believe last March? NO — needs History
a_rows_sample.statement: The state/history sufficiency boundary is drawn precisely: K alone answers what is currently held, what follows from an operation (congruence), whether structural/semantic invariants hold, and current epistemic status (recomputable from e); K alone CANNOT answer who asserted something and when, whether every admission was properly authorised (GovernanceValid(K,Gamma) needs History), or what was believed at a past point in time (needs History or a bitemporal interpretation of t).

a_rows_sample.anchor: K answers what is known. History answers how it came to be known and by whom. Neither reduces to the other, and T needs only the first.
a_rows_sample.statement: Governing principle stated as the resolution of the state/history boundary the programme has circled since the executed History(K)!=K counterexample: K answers what is known; History answers how it came to be known and by whom; neither reduces to the other, and the transformation function T needs only K.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The governing criterion is: F_i(H_1)=F_i(H_2) must imply F_i(\widehat T(H_1,c)) = F_i(\widehat T(H_2,c))
b_rows_sample.statement: A candidate Knowledge-State abstraction F_i:H->K_i is sufficient for a mandatory transformation T over admissible context c iff F_i(H1)=F_i(H2) implies F_i(That(H1,c))=F_i(That(H2,c)); strengthened to require an actual state-level transformation T_i:K_i x C -> K_i such that F_i(That(H,c)) = T_i(F_i(H),c) for all admissible H,c (a commuting square between history-level and state-level transformations).

b_rows_sample.anchor: In particular: Definition of K != Adequacy of K, and: Congruence criterion valid != KnowledgeOS satisfies congruence.
b_rows_sample.statement: Self-correction of the immediately preceding step: a mathematical definition of K, a candidate representation of K, an abstraction F:H->K, and the claim that F is sufficient for the transformation family are four distinct claims that must not be conflated; Step 258 wrongly treated K as already a well-defined state abstraction.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Not every operation has the form: T:K -> K. ... Assess:K x X -> Assessment ... Authorize:Actor x Action x Policy -> Decision
b_rows_sample.statement: Operations must first be classified into (1) knowledge-state transformations, (2) epistemic assessments, (3) governance operations, (4) audit/history operations, (5) observation operations; not every legitimate KnowledgeOS operation is an endomorphism T:K->K — e.g. Assess:K x X -> Assessment and Authorize:Actor x Action x Policy -> Decision are non-state-closing operations, and only state-transforming operations enter the primary congruence test.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Now introduce a revision rule dependent on lineage: Revise(x_1,x_2) is permitted only if: Origin(x_1) in ApprovedSources.
b_rows_sample.statement: Conditional counterexample sketch for candidate F_A (artifact-set state) under Revise: if revision eligibility depends on Origin(x1) (an approved-sources lineage rule) while F_A discards origin, two histories with equal F_A images can differ in whether a subsequent Revise is valid, which would falsify F_A's congruence — but this is CONDITIONAL, not PROVEN, unless the corpus actually establishes that revision eligibility depends on origin.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Merge is the strongest initial discriminator ... If the resulting provenance must distinguish Source_1 from Source_2, then F_A(\widehat{Merge}(H_A)) != F_A(\widehat{Merge}(H_B)).
b_rows_sample.statement: Conditional counterexample sketch for candidate F_A under Merge, described as the strongest initial discriminator among the tested operations: if two histories reach the same artifact x1 from different sources (Source_1 vs Source_2) with F_A(H_A)=F_A(H_B)={x1}, and a subsequent Merge(x1,x2) must record provenance distinguishing Source_1 from Source_2, then F_A fails congruence — again only if provenance is established as semantically observable by Merge, which the governing prompt requires testing (alongside evidence, replay, validation, implementation needs) before deciding whether Evidence/provenance belongs inside or outside K.

b_rows_sample.anchor: All transformations are K -> K | REFUTED as a universal assumption
b_rows_sample.statement: The results table explicitly marks the assumption that all KnowledgeOS transformations have signature K->K as REFUTED as a universal assumption (distinguished from the still-CANDIDATE status of F:H->K as a useful abstraction model, and from several UNRESOLVED items: whether history can be discarded, whether provenance must be inside or can remain outside K, whether the transformation family is closed, whether current K is globally sufficient, whether a minimal K exists).

b_rows_sample.anchor: We cannot perform a valid global congruence proof until the mandatory transformation family is itself sufficiently closed. ... the quantifier forall T in T has no determinate meaning if T is incomplete.
b_rows_sample.statement: Central negative result of the step: a valid global congruence proof is impossible while the mandatory transformation family T is not itself closed, because the universal quantifier 'for all T in T' is not well-defined over an incomplete set; this reinforces the required sequencing Transformation Inventory -> Semantic Classification -> Congruence, rather than jumping to K -> Congruence in isolation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A finite test set can establish: Congruent_{tested}(F). It does not automatically establish: Congruent_{global}(F).
b_rows_sample.statement: Local/tested congruence (survival of a finite, executed test set) must be distinguished from global congruence (a formal proof over the fully specified domain and transformation family); an executed test yields only 'evidence of survival', never 'proof of universal congruence'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This also explains why Step 260 must come after Step 259. Minimality asks whether K* is the coarsest sufficient abstraction. But we cannot establish sufficiency until we know which operations must be preserved.
b_rows_sample.statement: Sequencing principle: no valid minimality proof (Step 260, testing whether K* = H/equiv is the coarsest sufficient state abstraction) can precede the operation registry and congruence-matrix analysis (Step 259), since minimality presupposes knowledge of which operations a sufficient state must preserve.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A bounded context state is legitimate only if its externally observable behavior does not depend on information that the context has discarded. ... K1 equiv_K K2 must imply identical behavior under the context's published operations.
b_rows_sample.statement: DDD interpretation of the congruence criterion: a bounded-context state representation is legitimate only when its externally observable behavior under the context's published operations does not depend on information the context's state has discarded — i.e. the congruence test is a rigorous check for an accidentally omitted domain invariant, not mathematical decoration.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We must not assume: Statistical Sufficiency => KnowledgeOS Operational Sufficiency. That requires proof.
b_rows_sample.statement: Statistical interpretation: two histories can produce the same estimated distribution P_theta under a distributional candidate state F_E, yet still be distinguishable by a future transformation dependent on information not identifiable from that distribution; statistical sufficiency must not be assumed to imply KnowledgeOS operational sufficiency without separate proof.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 259 establishes the formal mechanism by which candidate Knowledge-State abstractions can be falsified, but it does not yet establish that any candidate abstraction is globally sufficient. ... if the quotient does not exist in the required usable form, that is a valid research result.
b_rows_sample.statement: Conservative step verdict: the congruence-falsification mechanism is established but no candidate is proven globally sufficient; Step 260 is set up to test — not assume — existence, uniqueness, representability, computability, decidability, composability, equality, membership and identity of the candidate minimal quotient K*=H/equiv (H1 equiv H2 iff no mandatory operation can distinguish them), explicitly allowing a negative result (the quotient not existing in usable form) as a valid outcome.

b_rows_sample.anchor: H1 ≈ H2 iff every permitted observation produces the same result: ∀O∈𝒪: O(H1)=O(H2). ... This is the relation already underlying Step 260's behavioral quotient.
b_rows_sample.statement: Observational equivalence for histories (H1 approx H2 iff every permitted observation O produces the same result) and for states (K1 approx K2 iff every permitted state observation agrees) is identified as the same relation already underlying Step 260's behavioral quotient; notably it does not require internal representations to be identical.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K1 ≡_K K2 ⟺ ∀O∈𝒪_K: O(K1)=O(K2) ... 𝒪_K is not yet completely closed. Therefore this is a candidate formal definition, not a completed theorem.
b_rows_sample.statement: Candidate formal definition of Knowledge-State equality as purely observational/behavioral: K1 equiv_K K2 iff every permitted state observation O in the (not-yet-closed) set O_K agrees on K1 and K2; explicitly a candidate, not a completed theorem, because O_K is not yet closed.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Equality → Congruence → Quotient → Minimality. This is the correct dependency direction.
b_rows_sample.statement: If K1 equiv_K K2 (no permitted observation distinguishes them) and all mandatory operations preserve that equivalence, equiv_K becomes the congruence relation needed for the minimal quotient K*=H/equiv (Step 260) — establishing the dependency direction Equality -> Congruence -> Quotient -> Minimality as correct.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Four capabilities have NO OWNER: C-5 separation attestation, C-10 knowledge distribution, C-14 policy enforcement, C-19 communication composition. INFERRED: these four, not the six roles, are the substance of ADR-AIP-04.
a_rows_sample.statement: Headline finding: of a 20-capability inventory (C-1..C-20) derived from evidence of what the platform actually does, four capabilities (C-5 separation attestation, C-10 knowledge distribution, C-14 policy enforcement, C-19 communication composition) have no declared owner -- proposed as the real substance of ADR-AIP-04, in contrast to the six proposed roles.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EKS-01: the HANDOFF token's tokenRef acted as the de-facto knowledge channel and taught a lane the superseded path. A lane was taught the old path by its workflow record's tokenRef.
a_rows_sample.statement: Finding F-5/F-5a: BC-7's HANDOFF tokenRef is performing de-facto knowledge distribution it does not own, evidenced by EKS-01 where a lane was taught a superseded path via its own workflow record's tokenRef -- the strongest evidence for a distinct C-10 (Knowledge Distribution) capability rather than 'Communication' in the ordinary sense.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Communication is two capabilities wearing one name. C-10 Knowledge Distribution -- a genuine, evidenced, unowned MECHANISM ... C-19 Communication Composition -- a STEWARDSHIP
a_rows_sample.statement: 'Communication' as commonly discussed is proposed to be two distinct capabilities: C-10 Knowledge Distribution (a genuine unowned mechanism, evidenced by EKS-01) and C-19 Communication Composition (a stewardship, failing the bounded-context test on language and reason-to-change); a single 'Communication Engineer' role would wrongly bind a mechanism gap and a reporting duty into one actor.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Distinguish, explicitly: ContextPublished, ContextSelected, ContextDelivered, ContextAvailable, ContextAcknowledged, ContextApplied, ContextVerified. Receipt is not proof of application or compliance.
a_rows_sample.statement: C-10's knowledge-distribution lifecycle is to be modelled as seven distinguished states (ContextPublished, ContextSelected, ContextDelivered, ContextAvailable, ContextAcknowledged, ContextApplied, ContextVerified); a receipt is never proof of application or compliance, only of a narrower claim.

type_signature.codomain: one of seven distinguished lifecycle states

a_rows_sample.anchor: that recurrence is itself evidence bearing on C-10 -- governed knowledge arriving outside the governed channel -- and the analysis may note it, but per AMD1 must not assume C-10 owns it.
a_rows_sample.statement: A pattern of substantive external input (a cited review, a 925-line brainstorming document, external research) repeatedly arriving outside the governed channel is recorded as evidence potentially bearing on C-10, but explicitly not assumed to be owned by C-10 without further decision.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C-5: YES existence, control-plane function category. C-10: NOT YET ESTABLISHED, deferred category. C-14: CONTESTED, deferred. C-19: YES, stewardship/cross-cutting category. The forbidden collapse is absent.
a_rows_sample.statement: Independent verification confirms the existence/category split was applied without the forbidden collapse for all four capabilities: C-5 exists (control-plane function), C-10's existence is NOT YET ESTABLISHED (category deferred), C-14's existence is CONTESTED (category deferred), C-19 exists (stewardship/cross-cutting), each argued from positive properties rather than derived from the other axis.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The four are not four candidate contexts. They are one CONTROL LOOP with four distinct capabilities in it. policy/knowledge DEFINED (BC-1) -> C-10 DELIVERS it to the gated session -> C-14 GATES the act -> C-19 EXPRESSES the outcome <- C-5 ATTESTS who acted
a_rows_sample.statement: Structural finding: C-5, C-10, C-14, C-19 are not four independent candidate bounded contexts but four capabilities within one control loop -- BC-1's policy/knowledge is delivered by C-10 to a gated session, C-14 gates the act, C-19 expresses the outcome, and C-5 attests who acted and how separately -- while still having four distinct reasons to change, so the relationship, not a merged boundary, is what explains them.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C-10 is NOT the whole path. Its smallest coherent boundary is APPLICABILITY + RECEIPT. ... What nothing owns is: (a) deciding WHICH governed knowledge is applicable to THIS assignment, and (b) evidencing that the executing session actually holds the CURRENT version.
a_rows_sample.statement: C-10's smallest coherent capability boundary is proposed to be applicability determination plus receipt (not the whole created->published->selected->retrieved->delivered->acknowledged->applied->verified path), since creation/publication is BC-1's, retrieval/bootstrap is BC-6's, and only applicability-determination and receipt-evidencing are genuinely unowned.

a_rows_sample.anchor: fails on 6 of 10 => a STEWARDSHIP / cross-cutting expression concern ... the only state that could make a Communication context real -- delivery-with-acknowledgement -- is C-10's receipt, not C-19's. building C-10 would REDUCE the case for a Communication context.
a_rows_sample.statement: C-19 fails a ten-part bounded-context test on six of ten criteria (own language, independent lifecycle, independent authority, authoritative state, distinct reason to change, audience/consent/channel concepts) and is classified a stewardship/cross-cutting expression concern; the one property that could give it authoritative state (delivery-with-acknowledgement) actually belongs to C-10, so realizing C-10 reduces rather than increases the case for a Communication bounded context.

a_rows_sample.anchor: two independent grounds: an ADOPTED invariant (INV-ATTR-2) that presupposes the capability, and the capability has been PERFORMED. C-10 satisfies neither limb.
a_rows_sample.statement: A two-limb existence test emerges from Amendment 1's C-5 analysis: a capability's existence is supported by (1) an ADOPTED invariant presupposing it, and/or (2) the capability having been PERFORMED at least once; C-5 satisfies both limbs (INV-ATTR-2 adopted; SB-1 clearance is a performed instance), while C-10 satisfies neither.

a_rows_sample.anchor: receipt <= application <= understanding <= compliance ... A receipt can only ever evidence ContextAcknowledged. ContextApplied and ContextVerified are different claims requiring different evidence, and no receipt can supply them.
a_rows_sample.statement: C-10's seven-state receipt model is elaborated with an explicit ceiling: a receipt can only ever evidence ContextAcknowledged, never ContextApplied or ContextVerified, and OQ-J is reformulated from a yes/no 'is the receipt authoritative' question into five separately-tested claims (delivery, possession, applicability, execution, compliance authority), of which a receipt can carry at most the first two.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Option C binds the receipt to an act the estate has never performed, that nobody owns, and that the analysis says a receipt cannot carry.
a_rows_sample.statement: Option C for C-10 receipt semantics is found unsatisfiable as worded, because it would require the receipt to reference an 'applicability decision' (ContextSelected) that never occurs and has no owner in the estate -- the same referent-gap defect noticed independently in several later documents.

a_rows_sample.anchor: establishes an applicability reference -- a pointer to decision A. does NOT establish the correctness of applicability -- whether A was right. A pointer to a judgement is not an assertion that the judgement was sound.
a_rows_sample.statement: C-10 Decision 1 (Option C) resolves OQ-J's authority defect by distinguishing an applicability REFERENCE (a pointer, which the receipt may carry) from applicability CORRECTNESS (whether the referenced judgement was sound, which the receipt does not establish) -- 'AUTHORITY IS CLAIM-SCOPED' is recorded as the invariant.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The decision commits the receipt to reference an applicability decision that the estate never produces. ... This is no longer an authority problem -- it is an existence problem about the referent.
a_rows_sample.statement: A distinct 'referent gap' (as opposed to the already-solved authority gap) is identified: the decided receipt is required to reference an applicability decision (ContextSelected) that the estate never actually produces and nobody owns, so a conforming receipt is not presently populatable -- left as PO/ARB's to decide (optional/null reference, vs. a standing obligation to build ContextSelected).

a_rows_sample.anchor: No typed KnowledgeDeliveryReceipt structure is adopted -- and, verified: no such type exists anywhere in the estate
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit confirmation that no typed receipt data structure (e.g. KnowledgeDeliveryReceipt) exists anywhere in the estate's code or docs; schema design is deferred to Architecture and is not created by this semantic decision.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Recommended: YES -- C-10 exists as a capability, with realization NONE and its outer boundary OPEN. The load-bearing argument is D1 itself. ... A decision fixing the authoritative claim boundary of C-10's artifact presupposes a subject for that artifact.
a_rows_sample.statement: Governance recommends C-10 existence = YES, arguing that D1's decided receipt-claim boundary presupposes a subject for that claim, supported by a distinct reason to change, a distinct outcome, and two genuinely unowned stages sharing one purpose (applicability + receipt) -- this recommendation is later overturned by the PO/ARB (S0120 D2) as conflating a decided semantic with a performed capability.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Of five activities: one occurs and is owned elsewhere; four do not occur at all. Evidence of C-10 having occurred: none
a_rows_sample.statement: Applying the ten-question existence test to the estate's evidence: of C-10's five constituent activities (applicability, delivery, acknowledgement, claim-scoped receipt, invalidation/reconciliation), only one occurs and it is owned by other contexts (BC-6/BC-7), while four never occur at all and have no owner -- the counter-evidence supporting the later NOT YET ESTABLISHED verdict.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The platform cannot attest a specified session execution. identity binding must NOT be placed inside C-10's authoritative state, because C-10 cannot establish it. It is C-5-shaped
a_rows_sample.statement: The sharpest finding in the D3 prep: a C-10 receipt's binding to a specific session execution can never be stronger than what INV-ATTR-1/INV-ATTR-2 permit (self-declared, not attested), so identity binding cannot be placed inside C-10's authoritative state -- it is C-5-shaped, and C-5 owns no attestation record either.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Adopting the receipt as authoritative state would supply limb one of the estate's existence test. A decision framed as constitutive would decide existence by the back door -- which this act forbids. Framed as a boundary specification, it does not.
a_rows_sample.statement: A distinction between a 'constitutive' decision (which would establish existence as a side effect) and a 'boundary specification' decision (which defines a candidate scope without establishing existence) is drawn, warning that D3 must be framed as the latter to avoid silently satisfying the D2 existence test.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C -- SPLIT. Fits every decided constraint. It matches OQ-J's 2-of-5 result ... applicability / transport / execution are already owned or already excluded
a_rows_sample.statement: Recommendation: Option C (SPLIT) for D3 -- C-10 would own only the receipt/attestation lifecycle and state (receipt identity, lifecycle state, invalidation, completeness), explicitly excluding applicability determination, delivery transport, session execution, identity binding, dispute adjudication, execution authority, and compliance/application.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Selecting is the decision itself, and every grant in this work item reserves it ... This is a decision-authority boundary, not a refusal of an assignment.
b_rows_sample.statement: A decision-authority boundary distinct from an independence-gate refusal is articulated: recording a PO/ARB decision option is not the same act as selecting among the options, and a governed process supplying a selection would itself be usurping the PO/ARB's reserved decision authority.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Option C binds the receipt to an act the estate has never performed, that nobody owns, and that the analysis says a receipt cannot carry.
b_rows_sample.statement: Option C for C-10 receipt semantics is found unsatisfiable as worded, because it would require the receipt to reference an 'applicability decision' (ContextSelected) that never occurs and has no owner in the estate -- the same referent-gap defect noticed independently in several later documents.

b_rows_sample.anchor: establishes an applicability reference -- a pointer to decision A. does NOT establish the correctness of applicability -- whether A was right. A pointer to a judgement is not an assertion that the judgement was sound.
b_rows_sample.statement: C-10 Decision 1 (Option C) resolves OQ-J's authority defect by distinguishing an applicability REFERENCE (a pointer, which the receipt may carry) from applicability CORRECTNESS (whether the referenced judgement was sound, which the receipt does not establish) -- 'AUTHORITY IS CLAIM-SCOPED' is recorded as the invariant.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'oq-j-receipt-authority-claim' POSSIBLY relates to 'capability-c10-knowledge-distribution' (batch B0003). Note: Reformulated from a single yes/no question into five separately-tested claims a C-10 receipt might be authoritative for (delivery, possession, applicability, execution, compliance); a receipt can carry at most the first two.
labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 2 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: PublishedContract_A -> Translation -> ConsumerModel_B; a context never exposes its internal model directly
a_rows_sample.statement: States the fundamental rule: InternalModel_A must never flow directly to InternalModel_B merely because another context needs information; instead PublishedContract_A -> Translation -> ConsumerModel_B.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Four interaction types Command/Query/Event/Observation; Intent != Fact; query preserves state; Observation !== DomainEvent
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes four non-interchangeable interaction types: Command X->Request ('please change something'), Query X->Information ('tell me something'), Event X->Fact ('something has happened'), Observation X->Report ('a source reported/measured something'). Example: AuthorizeDecision is a command (expresses intent), DecisionAuthorized is an event (records an accomplished fact) -- Intent != Fact. A query conceptually satisfies State_after=State_before while a command may produce State_after != State_before. Event immutability: once DecisionAuthorized has occurred it is never rewritten into DecisionRejected; instead a later event DecisionAuthorizationRevoked is emitted -- history is append-oriented. Observation != DomainEvent: an observation says 'source reports X', an event says 'domain state transition X occurred' -- example, CPU=98% is an Observation, not automatically ServerOverloaded (an interpretation/claim); preserves Observation -> Evidence -> Claim, never Observation === Truth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Contract algebra Γ_A=(Commands_A,Queries_A,Events_A,Observations_A); contract stability; Published Language must not become a global domain model
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a context's public contract as Gamma_A = (Commands_A, Queries_A, Events_A, Observations_A); consumers may depend on Gamma_A but not on Internal_A -- if Internal_A changes while Gamma_A does not, consumers should remain unaffected ('one of the most important architectural properties'). Adopts DDD's Published Language for an intentionally shared communication model, but warns it should not become a GlobalDomainModel -- it should contain only what the contract needs. Example DTO: DecisionAuthorized carries decisionId, decisionVersion, policyVersion, authorityReference, authorizedAt -- not the complete Decision aggregate; sending a Reference instead of an EntireAggregate reduces coupling, with additional information requested via explicit query if permitted -- but a bare reference does not guarantee the consumer later sees the same state, so critical events should carry the relevant immutable snapshot/version information.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Every contract needs a ContractVersion; SchemaCompatibility != SemanticCompatibility
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires ContractVersion (e.g. DecisionAuthorized.v1) with a safe-evolution rule Contract_v2 superset-of-or-equal RequiredSemantics(Contract_v1) where compatibility is intended, but argues semantic compatibility matters more than field compatibility: example, status='approved' silently changing meaning from 'technically reviewed' to 'legally authorized' keeps the schema identical while SemanticCompatibility=False -- therefore SchemaCompatibility != SemanticCompatibility, and a contract should define Meaning(field), not merely Type(field). Cross-context semantic translation must be explicit: T_AB(Approved_A) = TechnicallyReviewed_B, never silently Approved_B; the ACL owning this transformation protects SemanticIntegrity, not merely technical plumbing.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Contract invariants; cross-context query semantics (AuthorizationResult status includes Unknown != Denied)
a_rows_sample.statement: Each contract defines invariants I_Gamma (e.g. decisionId != empty, policyVersion != empty, authorizedAt != empty). Cross-context query example: DecisionContext asks Governance IsAuthorized(D)?, receiving AuthorizationResult=(decisionId, policyVersion, authority, status, validUntil) with status in {Authorized, Denied, Unknown, Expired} -- again Unknown != Denied -- and Decision Context must not reinterpret the response; the contract defines the semantics.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Temporal query contract: LiveQuery vs HistoricalQuery; AsOfTimestamp+KnowledgeVersion prevents a major failure mode
a_rows_sample.statement: A query like GetAuthorization(D) must define its temporal semantics -- AuthorizationNow(D) versus AuthorizationAt(D,t) are completely different; a historical query Query(K,t) ('what was known at time t') is essential for auditability and must return Result + AsOfTimestamp + KnowledgeVersion, otherwise 'as of' semantics are ambiguous. Distinguishes LiveQuery from HistoricalQuery and DecisionSnapshot from CurrentState: if asked 'why did the system authorize this change yesterday', a live query might now show Denied, which does not answer the historical question -- the correct answer must use State_yesterday.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Event contract fields including CorrelationID; CorrelationID != CausalRelation
a_rows_sample.statement: An event should identify What, When, Where/Context, Version, and Correlation; a CorrelationID lets a workflow trace (Request->Decision->Action->Outcome) be reconstructed, but CorrelationID != CausalRelation -- it merely identifies workflow lineage; Causes(A,B) remains a separately modeled relation, and correlation may support but does not establish causal investigation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Command semantics and idempotency key; commands may be rejected (Command != Event)
a_rows_sample.statement: A command should contain Intent + Target + Parameters + Actor + Correlation (example: AuthorizeDecision carries decisionId, requestedBy, reason, correlationId). A command does not guarantee a state transition -- Command -> Accepted or Command -> Rejected, reinforcing Command != Event. Commands with external side effects require an IdempotencyKey k, such that Execute(Command,k) repeated multiple times yields EffectiveExecution(k)=1.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Query consistency semantics and event delivery/ordering semantics (at-most/at-least/effectively-once; sequence numbers)
a_rows_sample.statement: A query must specify consistency semantics (e.g. ReadYourWrites vs EventuallyConsistent) when it affects meaning. Event delivery must distinguish AtMostOnce, AtLeastOnce, and EffectivelyOnce ('exactly once is often much harder than it appears in distributed systems'); KnowledgeOS's preferred strategy for critical domain events is AtLeastOnce + IdempotentConsumer, 'usually more robust than assuming magical exactly-once delivery'. Where order matters, a SequenceNumber (e.g. seq=10, seq=11) lets consumers detect gaps; if seq=11 arrives before seq=10, the consumer should not blindly apply it where the invariant requires ordering.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Contract algebra summary Γ={Cmd,Qry,Evt,Obs}, each with Schema+Semantics+Version+Invariant+TemporalMeaning+FailureSemantics
a_rows_sample.statement: Consolidates Gamma = {Cmd, Qry, Evt, Obs}, each carrying Schema + Semantics + Version + Invariant + TemporalMeaning + FailureSemantics -- 'much stronger than an API schema alone'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Full context-contract matrix across the seven Step-52 contexts
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies the algebra as a producer/consumer/contract matrix: Evidence->Knowledge (EvidencePublished), Knowledge->Causal (Claim/KnowledgeView), Knowledge->Decision (KnowledgeSnapshot), Causal->Decision (CausalAssessment), Decision->Governance (AuthorizationRequest), Governance->Decision (AuthorizationResult), Decision->Action (ActionRequest), Action->Evidence (OutcomeObservation), Outcome->Learning (LearningInput), Agent->Context (Command/Query). Notes not every row must be an event -- e.g. Knowledge->Decision may use a snapshot/query -- the architecture should choose Command, Query, or Event according to semantics. Producer owns the meaning of its Published Language; consumer owns its own interpretation (ConsumerModel).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Anti-pattern: architecture as pure event chains; forbidding shared mutable domain objects across contexts
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns an architecture consisting entirely of Event->Event->Event chains 'can become impossible to reason about' -- explicit domain boundaries and commands are still needed; the good default pattern is Command -> DomainTransition -> Event (e.g. AuthorizeDecision -> Governance -> DecisionAuthorized), with queries kept separate via Query -> Context -> ReadModel. Explicitly forbids sharing a mutable Claim object between Context A and Context B (either side could mutate semantics); only an ImmutableContract may cross the boundary, and messages crossing boundaries should preferably be immutable, especially for historical evidence and events.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CQRS/event-sourcing/microservices are implementation choices, not requirements ('no architecture astronautics')
a_rows_sample.statement: States KnowledgeOS naturally supports separate CommandModel and QueryModel but does not require full CQRS everywhere -- use it where the domain benefits. Warns against introducing event sourcing, CQRS, Kafka, graph databases, or microservices merely because they 'sound appropriate': each is an implementation choice; the invariant is DomainSemantics, not TechnologyName. The contract can be implemented via HTTP, gRPC, messaging, database, or in-process call -- the domain should not care.

a_rows_sample.anchor: BoundedContext != Microservice; modular-monolith-first is mathematically sufficient; deployment transformation preserves Γ_context
a_rows_sample.statement: States there is no mathematical requirement for microservices: KnowledgeOS can start as a ModularMonolith, which may initially be better because it gives strong module boundaries while avoiding premature distributed-system complexity, with Module_A -> Service_A extraction later if justified. States the critical principle BoundedContext != Microservice: a bounded context is a semantic boundary, a microservice is a deployment boundary -- contexts (evidence, semantic, knowledge, causal, decision, governance, learning) can live in one process initially, later split into separate services, without changing the fundamental domain model; the deployment transformation ModularMonolith -> DistributedSystem should preserve Gamma_context and ideally be an infrastructure transformation, not a semantic redesign.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Agent contract: agent as external Actor, cannot invent authoritative events; authority is domain-owned, not AI-capability-owned
a_rows_sample.statement: An agent is an external Actor: it receives Query, submits Command, receives Event/Result. The agent may request AuthorizeDecision but cannot claim DecisionAuthorized -- only the Governance Context can produce that authoritative event. States the important security property: authority is determined by domain ownership, not by AI capability.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Agent receives a structured KnowledgeView (provenance/temporal-scope/uncertainty/source), not a text blob; distinguishes KnowledgeOS from RAG; Proposal != Decision
a_rows_sample.statement: An agent should receive a KnowledgeView with Provenance, TemporalScope, Uncertainty, Source -- not merely a text blob; this is where KnowledgeOS becomes more powerful than RAG (which typically returns bare text chunks): KnowledgeOS returns StructuredKnowledge + Evidence + Provenance + TemporalValidity + Uncertainty. KnowledgeOS distinguishes an agent's generated Answer from an EvidenceBackedClaim, and similarly a Proposal is not a Decision -- the transition remains Proposal -> Evaluation -> Decision.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Ten falsification experiments for Step 53 context-contract algebra (all PASS)
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs ten falsification tests, all PASS: (1) can a consumer modify producer state directly? No; (2) can a command be mistaken for an event? The type system/contract should prevent it; (3) can an observation automatically become truth? No; (4) can two contexts use the same word differently? Yes, through explicit context semantics; (5) can an AI agent create an authoritative event? No; (6) can an event be silently rewritten? No; (7) can historical state be answered using current state? No, if historical semantics are requested; (8) can contract schema compatibility hide semantic incompatibility? The model explicitly rejects that assumption; (9) can the contexts initially run in one process? Yes; (10) can they later be distributed? Yes, provided contracts remain preserved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Formal context composition B_i=(M_i,Γ_i,I_i); Preserve(T_ij,I_required); LocalInvariant+ContractInvariant⇒GlobalInvariant links back to Step 48
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a context as B_i=(M_i,Gamma_i,I_i) (internal model, published contracts, invariants), a context interaction T_ij: Gamma_i -> M_j required to preserve semantics (Preserve(T_ij,I_required)), and the complete system as KOS = direct-sum_i B_i with explicit contracts Gamma_ij, with the goal LocalInvariant + ContractInvariant ⇒ GlobalInvariant -- explicitly connecting Step 53 back to Step 48's compositional correctness result. Declares STEP 53 -- PASS and states the important result is not merely that communication works but that 'KnowledgeOS boundaries are semantic and contractual, not merely technical'. Opens Step 54 (Mathematical Types -> DDD Domain Types -> Executable Contracts): deriving an actual type system from P={Entity,State,Event,Observation,Proposition,Relation,Policy,Action} down to concrete types (EntityId, Observation, Evidence, Claim, Relation, KnowledgeSnapshot, Policy, Decision, Authorization, Action, Outcome) each with explicit Invariant, Ownership, Lifecycle, Version, Provenance, Contract -- 'the point at which our mathematical architecture can begin to translate directly into the actual KnowledgeOS software design'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Primitive ownership must follow domain responsibility, not one giant knowledge domain
b_rows_sample.statement: States the kernel primitives P={Entity,State,Event,Observation,Proposition,Relation,Policy,Action} do not imply one aggregate or one bounded context: primitive ownership must follow domain responsibility -- 'KnowledgeOS must not become one giant knowledge domain'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Seven candidate bounded contexts: Evidence, Semantic, Knowledge, Causal, Decision, Governance, Learning
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a candidate (not final) map of seven bounded contexts, each defined by a responsibility question and owned concepts: Evidence Context ('what was observed, from where, when, with what integrity?' owns Observation, Evidence, Source, EvidenceIntegrity; central invariant: evidence cannot be silently mutated -- correction creates a new state/version/event; must not own business decisions); Semantic Context ('what does a concept mean in a bounded context?' owns Meaning, Context, SemanticMapping via MapsTo(A,B,C); StringEquality != SemanticEquality); Knowledge Context ('what propositions are believed, under what evidence/epistemic status?' owns Claim, Hypothesis, KnowledgeState, Uncertainty; Evidence != Knowledge -- evidence supports knowledge, knowledge is an interpretation/epistemic state over evidence; K_t={C1,...,Cn} with per-claim Status/Scope/Validity/Uncertainty/Provenance); Causal Context ('what causal relationships are justified by evidence and model?' owns CausalModel, CauseRelation, Intervention, Counterfactual; consumes but does not own evidence -- CausalContext->EvidenceContext is a dependency, not ownership); Decision Context ('given state/knowledge/policy/constraints, what decision should be proposed?' owns Decision, DecisionBasis, DecisionContract, DecisionSnapshot; Decision != Authorization -- a proposal may exist without permission to execute); Governance Context ('which policies/authorities/governance rules apply?' owns Policy, Authority, Authorization, PolicyVersion; should not own domain truth, e.g. not decide 'the system is technically healthy' -- it determines what may be done given the relevant facts); Learning Context ('how should the system revise models/knowledge from experience?' owns LearningProcess, DriftDetection, ModelCandidate, ModelPromotion; can propose K_t->K_{t+1} but must not rewrite K_t -- historical state remains owned by the knowledge/history mechanism).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Each context must answer 'what does it have authority to change'; 'everything' means the boundary is wrong
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives an important DDD boundary test: each context should answer what it has authority to change; if the answer is 'everything', the boundary is wrong.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Aggregate boundary criterion: Invariant + Consistency + TransactionBoundary, not one aggregate per noun
b_rows_sample.statement: Warns against the common DDD mistake of creating an aggregate per noun (ClaimAggregate, EvidenceAggregate, SourceAggregate, ModelAggregate, PolicyAggregate, ...); aggregate boundaries must instead follow Invariant + Consistency + TransactionBoundary. Requires an aggregate to guarantee State_valid after every successful domain operation: I(A_t) ∧ ValidCommand ⇒ I(A_{t+1}). Gives a mathematical criterion: an aggregate should ideally contain the state necessary to enforce a local invariant I_A(S_A); if an invariant requires S_A+S_B+S_C every time, the boundary may be wrong, or the invariant is actually a cross-context policy.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Cross-context invariants resolved via contracts (Query/Result), never by merging aggregates
b_rows_sample.statement: Example cross-context invariant Execute(Action) ⇒ Authorized(Decision) spans DecisionContext and GovernanceContext; these must not be forced into one aggregate. Instead contexts communicate through a Contract: DecisionContext -> AuthorizationQuery, receiving AuthorizationResult -- this preserves ownership (Governance owns Authorization, Decision owns Decision; neither steals the other's model). Depicts a logical context-map flow Evidence -> Knowledge -> {Causal, and Semantic feeding Decision} -> Decision -> Governance -> Action -> Outcome -> Learning -> back to Knowledge, explicitly 'a logical flow, not necessarily synchronous runtime communication'. Anti-corruption layers ACL_AB translate Model_A -> Model_B preserving the semantic contract; example: Evidence Context's Observation(source,timestamp,value) maps to Knowledge Context's Evidence(proposition,scope,relevance) via SemanticTransformation, not FieldToField mapping.

b_rows_sample.anchor: AI agents as external actors, not domain owners; agent identity != knowledge identity; multi-agent disagreement preserved
b_rows_sample.statement: An AI agent should not directly manipulate another context's internal state: Agent -> ApplicationPort -> DomainOperation, preserving invariants; the agent may Observe, Query, Propose, RequestAction, but ownership remains with the domain. Gives the correct AI architecture as AI Agent -> Use Case/Port -> Bounded Context -> Domain Rules -> Invariant -> State Change (not LLM -> Database directly). States the key interpretation: KnowledgeOS is not the agent, it provides the epistemic and governance substrate on which agents operate; an agent requests RelevantKnowledge(Context,Time), receives K_t, proposes D, and the Decision Context evaluates it -- AgentProposal -> DecisionValidation, never AgentProposal -> Production directly. Different agent harnesses (Claude, Codex, etc.) interact through the same KnowledgeOS contracts ('agent symmetry'); knowledge belongs to KnowledgeOS, not to any specific agent, so Agent identity != Knowledge identity, and multiple agents (A1..An) can produce different hypotheses (H1..Hn) with disagreement preserved as Conflict(H_A,H_B) rather than automatically resolved by majority.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Agent provenance requirements (AgentID/ModelVersion/PromptVersion/EvidenceSnapshot) for auditability; domain model stays AI-provider-independent
b_rows_sample.statement: Every AI-generated artifact should identify AgentID, ModelVersion, Prompt/InstructionVersion, and EvidenceSnapshot where required by the assurance level, enabling auditability via Agent -> Decision -> KnowledgeSnapshot -> Evidence traversal. The domain model must remain AI-provider-independent (no 'if Claude then...' branching in the domain); InferenceProvider is an infrastructure/application concern.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Command != Event; trust boundary: external actors request, only authoritative domain logic commits
b_rows_sample.statement: Domain events (ClaimValidated, DecisionAuthorized, ActionExecuted, OutcomeObserved, KnowledgeRevised) describe something that has happened; commands describe a request ('please do this') -- this distinction must remain: Command != Event. An agent may issue RequestDecision but must not fabricate DecisionAuthorized; only the authoritative domain process emits that event. States the trust-boundary invariant: external actors may request domain transitions, but only authoritative domain logic may commit them.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Primitive-ownership audit: no primitive requires a global 'KnowledgeOS' owner
b_rows_sample.statement: Tests whether every mathematical primitive has a legitimate context owner: Entity identity -> Domain/Semantic context; State -> owning domain context; Event -> owning domain context; Observation -> Evidence; Proposition -> Knowledge; Relation -> owning relation context; Policy -> Governance; Action -> owning domain/operation context. Concludes 'no primitive requires a global owner called KnowledgeOS. That is a very healthy result.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Twelve falsification experiments for Step 52 DDD mapping (all PASS)
b_rows_sample.statement: Runs twelve falsification tests, all PASS: (1) can Evidence Context change Governance Policy? No; (2) can Learning Context rewrite historical evidence? No; (3) can an AI agent directly mutate aggregate state? No; (4) can Decision Context authorize itself? No, if Governance owns authorization; (5) can Semantic Context redefine domain invariants? No, it defines mappings/meaning, not domain behavior; (6) can Causal Context alter raw observations? No; (7) can two contexts use the same word with different meanings? Yes -- that is exactly why bounded contexts exist; (8) can two agents disagree? Yes, disagreement is preserved; (9) can a new AI provider replace another without changing domain logic? Yes, if it implements the appropriate port; (10) can KnowledgeOS run without an LLM? Yes -- the deterministic kernel and domain contexts remain meaningful, so 'LLM is an optional reasoning mechanism, not the architectural foundation'; (11) can KnowledgeOS run with multiple AI providers? Yes; (12) can the core mathematical engine run on a normal PC? Yes for finite bounded workloads, with heavy computation delegated through infrastructure ports.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 52 verdict: KnowledgeOS != God Context; avoid God Aggregate; opens Step 53 Context Contract Algebra
b_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 52 -- PASS: a candidate DDD decomposition compatible with the mathematical kernel, having avoided the major architectural trap KnowledgeOS != God Context ('KnowledgeOS must be a system of bounded contexts, not a single bounded context'). Also warns against a God Aggregate (a KnowledgeAggregate containing everything, causing high contention, difficult transactions, poor scalability, difficult verification); each context should have OwnState, OwnInvariants, OwnLanguage, OwnPersistenceModel, communicating via explicit contracts and domain events. Depicts the resulting layered architecture (AI Agents -> Application -> KnowledgeOS Core [seven contexts] -> Ports -> Storage/Compute/External Systems) with agents sitting above the contexts. Opens Step 53 (Context Contract Algebra): what exactly crosses a bounded-context boundary (Command, Query, DomainEvent, IntegrationEvent, DTO, SemanticTranslation, InvariantContract), needed to avoid the architecture degenerating into shared mutable objects and implicit coupling, and to derive a concrete DDD Context Map + API/Event Contract model bridging the mathematical architecture to actual software modules, APIs, events, databases, and AI-agent interfaces.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Full context-contract matrix across the seven Step-52 contexts
b_rows_sample.statement: Applies the algebra as a producer/consumer/contract matrix: Evidence->Knowledge (EvidencePublished), Knowledge->Causal (Claim/KnowledgeView), Knowledge->Decision (KnowledgeSnapshot), Causal->Decision (CausalAssessment), Decision->Governance (AuthorizationRequest), Governance->Decision (AuthorizationResult), Decision->Action (ActionRequest), Action->Evidence (OutcomeObservation), Outcome->Learning (LearningInput), Agent->Context (Command/Query). Notes not every row must be an event -- e.g. Knowledge->Decision may use a snapshot/query -- the architecture should choose Command, Query, or Event according to semantics. Producer owns the meaning of its Published Language; consumer owns its own interpretation (ConsumerModel).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Agent contract: agent as external Actor, cannot invent authoritative events; authority is domain-owned, not AI-capability-owned
b_rows_sample.statement: An agent is an external Actor: it receives Query, submits Command, receives Event/Result. b_rows_sample.statement: No rule is violated (authorization still correctly requires MATCH), but the field name invites a human reader to conflate eligibility with authorization -- a legibility/naming finding, not a safety finding.
