a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision power is not the same thing as knowledge, and it is not the same thing as authority.
a_rows_sample.statement: From a book framing decisions as Aims->Information->Evaluation->Decision, Decision Power is defined as 'the bounded capability to choose among available alternatives under a mandate, using available information and evaluation, while carrying responsibility for the choice' -- explicitly distinct from both knowledge and authority; Knowledge informs Decision, which exercises Decision Power, which produces Action, but these are not ownership relationships (possessing evidence does not imply may-decide; having decision authority does not imply having all required knowledge).

a_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionalSpace
a_rows_sample.statement: DecisionalSpace is proposed as first-class: 'the set of choices that an actor is actually permitted and able to make in a given context,' richer than a bare role label; example: Architect A's DecisionalSpace lists Domain structure=ALLOWED, API contract=ALLOWED, Security policy=CONSULT, Production deployment=NOT_ALLOWED, Budget=NOT_ALLOWED.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision Power = Authority + Decisional Space + Available Alternatives + Information Access + Evaluation Capability + Resource Capability + Accountability - Constraints
a_rows_sample.statement: Decision Power is bounded by Authority/Mandate, Policy/Constitution, Scope, Time, Preconditions, Resources, Risk limits, and Accountability; six lenses (Governance/Knowledge/Reasoning/Agency/Risk/Accountability) each answer a distinct question (who may decide / what can be known / how was the choice justified / what choices are available / which choices are tolerable / who bears responsibility); the resulting formula (Authority+DecisionalSpace+Alternatives+InformationAccess+EvaluationCapability+ResourceCapability+Accountability-Constraints) is explicitly a conceptual model, not a mathematical formula -- a numerical 'decision power score' is explicitly rejected.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionRight
a_rows_sample.statement: DecisionRight is preferred over 'DecisionPower' as the kernel term (power sounds psychological/sociological): 'a governed entitlement of an actor to select or reject an option within a defined decisional space,' with fields Actor/Subject/Scope/PermittedActions/Constraints/Accountability, illustrated by example DR-17 (Architecture Committee; approve/reject/return-for-revision; constitutional rules/evidence requirements/quorum).

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would not necessarily persist DecisionPower as a primitive.
a_rows_sample.statement: DecisionPower is proposed as a derived concept, not a persisted primitive: DecisionPower(actor, context, time) computed from DecisionRights + Mandates + Constraints + Delegations + CurrentState, fitting the deterministic architecture direction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision power must be derivable from explicit rights and constraints; it must never be inferred merely from role, knowledge, seniority, or AI capability.
a_rows_sample.statement: Candidate constitutional invariant: decision power must be derivable from explicit rights and constraints, never inferred merely from role, knowledge, seniority, or AI capability -- 'AI knows enough' != 'AI may decide,' and 'CEO knows less about architecture' != 'CEO has no authority'; knowledge and authority are orthogonal dimensions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision support capability does not automatically imply decision authority.
a_rows_sample.statement: A 1998 source claim that computers can shape aims, provide/evaluate information and present options but do not possess the value judgment required for a 'true decision' is explicitly NOT imported as a KnowledgeOS truth (flagged as a dated philosophical/managerial position), but the underlying architectural insight is kept: decision support capability does not automatically imply decision authority; an AI Agent may discover/analyse evidence, generate/evaluate alternatives, recommend, and simulate consequences, without exercising a DecisionRight unless governance explicitly grants it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: three different AI modes
a_rows_sample.statement: Three AI decision modes distinguished: Mode 1 Advisory (AI->Recommendation->Human Decision), Mode 2 Delegated decision (Governance->DecisionRight->AI->Decision), Mode 3 Deterministic execution (Policy->Rule->Condition->Automatic Action) -- Mode 3 may not even be a 'decision' in the source's sense, since the book distinguishes genuine decisions from automatic acts/routine operations; DecisionKind values proposed: ConsideredDecision/DelegatedDecision/EmergencyDecision/DeferredDecision/AutomaticDetermination/Recommendation, with Recommendation != Decision and AutomaticDetermination != Human Decision as key semantic distinctions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision not to decide
a_rows_sample.statement: Four legitimate reasons to not decide are extracted (insufficient information; parity between options; deliberate preservation of options; inability/unsuitability to decide now); a null choice must not be modeled as an error but as DecisionOutcome{Chosen(option), Deferred(reason), Rejected, Escalated}, e.g. Decision D42 Status=DEFERRED Reason=INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE Missing=Network topology evidence Next condition=Infrastructure evidence received.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionReadiness
a_rows_sample.statement: Connecting to the prior Question->Inquiry->Evidence->Hypothesis->Assessment model, DecisionReadiness is introduced between Inquiry and Decision, checking RequiredEvidenceSatisfied/RequiredQuestionsAnswered/ContradictionsResolved/AuthorityPresent/AlternativesKnown/RiskAssessmentComplete/PreconditionsSatisfied, gating NOT-READY (defer/escalate/gather evidence) vs READY (decision permitted).

a_rows_sample.anchor: what information was actually considered in the decision
a_rows_sample.statement: Information must be evaluated before becoming decision input: a validity checklist (internal consistency, objectivity, completeness, context, source prestige, expertise, focus) gives Evidence->EvidenceAssessment->DecisionInput->Decision (not Evidence->Decision directly), so KnowledgeOS can preserve what information was actually considered in the decision -- critical for audit, since only some of many available facts are relevant/valid/current/understood/applicable.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionBasis
a_rows_sample.statement: DecisionBasis proposed as first-class (Aims/RelevantEvidence/Assessments/Alternatives/Risks/Assumptions/Constraints/Values/Reasoning), with Decision based-on-> DecisionBasis, structured rather than a natural-language 'rationale' string which is merely a representation of the actual (structured) basis.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Fact != Value != Preference != Constraint
a_rows_sample.statement: Decisions without an Aim/Objective become pseudo-decisions lacking coherence/motivation/focus (though 'unconscious aim' is explicitly not imported); competing aims (e.g. maximize reliability vs minimize cost vs release quickly) introduce a Tradeoff relation (Aim->Criterion->AlternativeEvaluation->Tradeoff->Decision); Fact, Value, Preference, and Constraint must be kept as distinct concepts (example: 'migration takes 4 weeks' fact vs 'minimize operational risk' value vs 'must not exceed 2 weeks' constraint vs 'team prefers Kubernetes' preference) since mixing them makes a decision system opaque.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Risk mitigation can enlarge effective decision space.
a_rows_sample.statement: Risk (mismatch between intention/achievement, expectation/consequence, cause/effect) introduces DecisionExposure (ExpectedOutcome/Uncertainty/Risk/Contingency) and a per-actor RiskAuthority threshold (e.g. Architect=LOW cannot approve a HIGH-risk decision; Committee=HIGH may); contingency planning (fallback/mitigation/insurance/reversible action) can enlarge DecisionalSpace dynamically (example: without rollback a deploy is too risky, with rollback it becomes acceptable) -- risk mitigation can enlarge effective decision space.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionRight must be contextual and temporal
a_rows_sample.statement: DecisionRight must be contextual and temporal (DecisionRight+Context+Time+State determines effective authority -- an actor may hold a right today but not tomorrow, or only during a specific phase); Delegation is explicit (Granted/Delegated/Restricted/Suspended/Revoked/Expired), and delegation is explicitly NOT equivalent to transfer of accountability unless governance says so.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DecisionRight != DecisionReadiness
a_rows_sample.statement: Organisational secrecy/information asymmetry can create a governance defect where an actor holds DecisionRight but lacks accessible RequiredEvidence, meaning the actor has authority but lacks decision capacity -- DecisionRight != DecisionReadiness; local decision space (decentralised operational units) is bounded by global governance/franchise rules, giving GlobalConstraint->LocalDecisionRight->LocalDecision without the local actor owning the global policy.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Authorized but not ready.
a_rows_sample.statement: Three distinct questions are made explicit: Decision Right ('May I decide?'), Decision Capacity ('Can I reasonably decide?'), Decision Readiness ('Should I decide now?'); example: an Architect with DecisionRight=YES, DecisionCapacity=YES, DecisionReadiness=NO (critical security evidence missing) should be reported as 'Authorized but not ready,' more precise than 'cannot decide.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: KOS-DP-01 -- Decision Sovereignty
a_rows_sample.statement: KOS-DP-01 Decision Sovereignty: KnowledgeOS may establish, preserve, evaluate, and expose the grounds, constraints, alternatives, risks, and readiness conditions surrounding a decision, but must not infer or grant decision authority from knowledge possession, reasoning capability, recommendation quality, or system access.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KOS-DP-02 -- Explicit Decision Right
a_rows_sample.statement: KOS-DP-02 Explicit Decision Right: a decision is authoritative only when the actor exercising it possesses an applicable DecisionRight within the relevant context, scope, state, and time; example: an AI saying 'Approve architecture' is not a decision, an AI submitting 'Recommendation: approve' is a recommendation, and an authorized ARB approving is an authoritative decision.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KOS-DP-03 -- Recommendation/Decision Separation
a_rows_sample.statement: KOS-DP-03 Recommendation/Decision Separation: a recommendation, evaluation, prediction, or automatically generated outcome must not be represented as a decision unless a valid decision act has occurred -- proposed as one of the most important AI-agent safeguards.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Steps 91-96 established implementation->concurrency->failure->adversarial behavior->privacy->evolution. But organizations are not machines. Can responsibility, authority, disagreement, escalation and collective decision-making be represented as first-class semantics?
b_rows_sample.statement: Frames Step 97's central question: whether responsibility, authority, disagreement, escalation, and collective decision-making can be first-class KnowledgeOS semantics rather than informal organizational assumptions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.1 — The organization becomes part of the system model ... Person, AIAgent, Role, Team, Organization, Authority. These are not interchangeable.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Person, AIAgent, Role, Team, Organization, and Authority as non-interchangeable entities, replacing the generic actor A.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.2 — Experiment 1: person versus role ... Alice may occupy role ArchitectureApprover during [t1,t2]. Expected: the authority belongs to the role assignment, not permanently to the person. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: authority belongs to a temporal role assignment (Alice as ArchitectureApprover during [t1,t2]), not permanently to the person; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.3 — Role assignment is temporal ... Assignment(P,R,t). Authority(P,R,t) depends on whether the assignment is valid at time t.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines temporal role assignment Assignment(P,R,t), with Authority(P,R,t) depending on the assignment's validity at t.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.4 — Experiment 2 ... Alice was ArchitectureApprover until t1. She issues an approval at t2>t1. Expected: the approval cannot automatically inherit the old authority. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: an approval issued after Alice's role expired (t2>t1) cannot inherit the expired authority; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.5 — Delegation ... A→Delegate→B. We need to know what authority was delegated, to whom, for what scope, for how long, under what conditions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines delegation A→Delegate→B, requiring explicit scope, recipient, duration, and conditions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.6 — Experiment 3 ... Alice delegates Approve(ProjectA) to Bob. Bob attempts Approve(ProjectB). Expected: delegation does not automatically extend beyond its declared scope. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: a ProjectA-scoped delegation does not extend to ProjectB; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.7 — Authority composition ... Authority(B,X) through a chain A→Delegation→B. But the chain must remain valid. If Authority(A,X)=False, then Delegate(A,B,X) cannot legitimately create Authority(B,X).
b_rows_sample.statement: States delegation chains must remain valid: Authority(A,X)=False means Delegate(A,B,X) cannot legitimately create Authority(B,X).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.8 — Experiment 4 ... Alice has no authority over production deployment. Alice delegates ProductionDeployment to Bob. Expected: Bob does not acquire authority from an unauthorized delegation. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: Bob does not acquire ProductionDeployment authority from Alice's unauthorized delegation; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.9 — Responsibility is different from authority ... Developer→ResponsibleForImplementation but Developer↛AuthorizedForProductionApproval.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Responsibility (e.g. ResponsibleForImplementation) from Authority (e.g. AuthorizedForProductionApproval) — an actor can hold one without the other.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.10 — Experiment 5 ... Developer prepares a change and is responsible for implementation quality. But governance requires an independent approver. Expected: preparation does not imply approval authority. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: preparing a change (responsibility) does not imply authority to approve it; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.11 — Responsibility assignment ... Responsibility(A,X,t) and separately Authority(A,X,t). These may overlap, but they are not identical.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines Responsibility(A,X,t) as distinct from, though possibly overlapping with, Authority(A,X,t).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.12 — Accountability ... Accountability(A,X): who is answerable for the outcome? Responsibility ≠ Authority ≠ Accountability.
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces Accountability(A,X) as a third distinct concept: Responsibility ≠ Authority ≠ Accountability.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.13 — Experiment 6 ... AI performs an action. Human manager authorized the AI. Expected: the AI may be the executing actor, while organizational accountability may remain with the responsible human role. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: an AI executing an action leaves organizational accountability with the responsible human role, not the AI; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.14 — AI cannot erase organizational accountability ... Delegating execution to AI does not automatically delegate organizational accountability. The exact allocation is a governance question, but it must be explicit.
b_rows_sample.statement: States delegating execution to AI does not automatically delegate organizational accountability; the allocation is a governance question that must be explicit.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.15 — Experiment 7 ... AI makes a recommendation. Human approves it. Expected: the system records separately AIRecommendation and HumanDecision. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: an AI recommendation and the resulting human decision must be recorded as two separate objects; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.16 — Collective decisions ... D=f(V_1,...,V_n). Majority(V), Unanimity(V), WeightedVote(V).
b_rows_sample.statement: Restates collective-decision aggregation D=f(V_1..V_n) via Majority, Unanimity, or WeightedVote rules.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.17 — Experiment 8 ... Committee has 5 members. Votes: 3 Yes, 2 No. Rule: Majority. Expected: Decision=Yes. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8 confirms a simple majority vote (3-2) yields Decision=Yes under a Majority rule; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.18 — Majority does not mean truth ... Majority ≠ Truth. A majority produces a legitimate decision only because the governance constitution defines the rule.
b_rows_sample.statement: Restates Majority ≠ Truth: a majority vote is legitimate only because the constitution defines that rule, not because it establishes truth.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 97.19 — Experiment 9 ... Five experts vote 5 No. Evidence strongly establishes Risk=True. Expected: the unanimous vote does not make Risk=False. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 9: a unanimous 5-No vote does not make Risk=False when evidence strongly establishes Risk=True; result PASS.

b_aliases: Human-AI Organizations, Responsibility and Collective Intelligence (Step 97)

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'human-ai-organization-responsibility-model' POSSIBLY relates to 'decision-power-model-lens' (batch B0024). Note: Step 97: models organizations as first-class KnowledgeOS semantics. Distinct Person/Role/Team/Organization/Authority; temporal role assignment and scoped delegation; Responsibility!=Authority!=Accountability with AI-execution-does-not-transfer-accountability; dissent as first-class KnowledgeArtifact; two independent assurance dimensions ProceduralValidity vs EpistemicSupport; escalation as legitimate PendingHigherAuthority state; human override of AI as first-class provenance event; argumentation structure and UnresolvedConflict as legitimate status; escalation graphs preserving full history; Decision!=Fact (decisions as scoped institutional facts, not universal truth); organizational ontology; AI agent identity/non-repudiable attribution; OrganizationalStructure!=DomainStructure; executable organizational-orphan/authority-orphan/single-point-of-knowledge-failure detection; and OrgKnowledge(t) epistemic state. Builds directly on the pre-existing collective-choice-aggregation-model and decision-power-model-lens.

a_rows_sample.anchor: O_t -> E_t(p|C,M) -> R_t(p|E,F,C,M) -> D_t(p) -> F_t ... Determination is the missing mathematical object in the current framework.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes the full research pipeline O_t -> E_t(p|C,M) -> R_t(p|E,F,C,M) -> D_t(p) -> F_t (observation, conditional evidence assessment, conditional reasoning, determination, fact), identifying D_t as the determination and concluding that Determination is the missing mathematical object in the current framework, since the prior pipeline treated Observation->Evidence->Fact as deterministic rather than making each stage explicitly conditional on context/time/model/rules/assumptions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(F\mid O_t,C_t,M_t,F_{<t},A_t) where A_t represents assumptions. This is not a recommendation that the Kernel should store this probability. It is a research question about what the probabilistic regime needs.
a_rows_sample.statement: The framework's P(F|O) is too simplistic because the same observation can support different propositions depending on context, interpretation, prior facts, model, measurement method, source reliability, time, and assumptions; proposes P(F|O_t,C_t,M_t,F_{<t},A_t) instead, explicitly framed as a research question about probabilistic-regime requirements, not a Kernel storage recommendation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: certainty of the rule != certainty of its premises != certainty of the conclusion. This is precisely the combination problem that the framework identifies but hasn't yet solved.
a_rows_sample.statement: Challenges the framework's use of the word 'established' for facts feeding logic/rules: a fact can have a graded epistemic state (e.g. P(F1)=0.8) even while the logical rule F1 and F2 => K applying to it is completely valid; therefore certainty of the rule, certainty of its premises, and certainty of the conclusion are three distinct things -- this is the combination problem the framework identifies but has not yet solved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Layer 1 -- uncertainty in extraction: O -> F, e.g. P(F|O)=0.8. Layer 2 -- uncertainty propagated through reasoning: given P(F1)=0.8 and F1=>K, we need to determine the epistemic state of K. ... How does uncertainty in premises interact with logical structure?
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies two distinct uncertainty layers: Layer 1, uncertainty in extraction (O->F, e.g. P(F|O)=0.8), and Layer 2, uncertainty propagated through reasoning (given P(F1)=0.8 and a rule F1=>K, the epistemic state of K is not automatically P(K)=0.8 and requires a combination semantics); the real underlying problem is how uncertainty in premises interacts with logical structure -- more fundamental than choosing among Bayesian/fuzzy/Dempster-Shafer.

a_rows_sample.anchor: uncertainty representation; conditional structure; combination rule; temporal aspect; conflict handling; ignorance representation. I would not call these invariants. They are dimensions along which the frameworks differ. ... We need a stricter definition of invariant: I(X)=I(Y) under some legitimate transformation between representations.
a_rows_sample.statement: Challenges the framework's list of cross-framework commonalities (uncertainty representation, conditional structure, combination rule, temporal aspect, conflict handling, ignorance representation) being called 'invariants': since Bayesian != Dempster-Shafer != Fuzzy != Argumentation in their uncertainty semantics, 'all frameworks represent uncertainty' establishes only a common research concern, not a mathematical invariant. Proposes the stricter test: an invariant must satisfy I(X)=I(Y) under some legitimate transformation between representations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: There may be a common algebraic structure underlying all these frameworks, e.g. lattice or measure-theoretic structure. I would mark this highly speculative. ... P(p) and mu(p) and mu_fuzzy(p) and Acceptable(p) may not be representations of one common mathematical object. They could represent different epistemic properties.
a_rows_sample.statement: Marks the framework's proposed 'common algebraic structure' (e.g. a lattice or measure-theoretic structure unifying all evidence-combination frameworks) as highly speculative and premature: before seeking a common algebra one must establish that the objects being represented (P(p), mu(p), mu_fuzzy(p), Acceptable(p)) are actually the same kind of thing -- they could instead represent different epistemic properties, which is exactly the danger the research has been trying to avoid.

a_rows_sample.anchor: First: What is the epistemic object? Second: What is the determination operation? Third: What does each regime represent? Fourth: When can two representations be considered equivalent? Fifth: What survives those equivalences? Only then do we ask: What is invariant?
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a safer six-step research ordering before asking about invariance: first, what is the epistemic object; second, what is the determination operation; third, what does each regime represent; fourth, when can two representations be considered equivalent; fifth, what survives those equivalences; only then, what is invariant.

a_rows_sample.anchor: E_t(p)=(proposition, support, justification, status, uncertainty, time). ... Bayesian theory may primarily represent uncertainty. Argumentation represents support/attack. Non-monotonic logic represents defeasible status. Epistemic logic represents knowledge relations. Temporal logic represents temporal truth. Measurement theory represents numerical attributes. These may be different dimensions of an epistemic state, rather than competing representations of one scalar object.
a_rows_sample.statement: Hypothesizes that epistemic state itself needs decomposition rather than being a generic scalar output E in script-E: E_t(p)=(proposition,support,justification,status,uncertainty,time). Under this hypothesis, different mathematical frameworks may each be capturing a different DIMENSION of epistemic state rather than competing representations of one scalar object: Bayesian theory primarily represents uncertainty, argumentation represents support/attack, non-monotonic logic represents defeasible status, epistemic logic represents knowledge relations, temporal logic represents temporal truth, and measurement theory represents numerical attributes. Explicitly framed as a hypothesis needing testing, not a proposed Kernel model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: How should conditional evidence and conditional reasoning combine to produce an epistemic state? I would retain that. But add: What are the distinct components of the epistemic state being produced? And then: Which components are regime-specific and which are regime-independent?
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the central research question: retains 'how should conditional evidence and conditional reasoning combine to produce an epistemic state', and adds two further questions -- what are the distinct components of the epistemic state being produced, and which components are regime-specific versus regime-independent.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Is Knowledge probabilistic? No. Is the extraction of Knowledge probabilistic? Some extraction processes are probabilistic. Is the resulting epistemic state probabilistic? It can be represented probabilistically, but that is regime-dependent. ... What exactly is being represented by the probability?
a_rows_sample.statement: Traces the evolving answer to a recurring question across the discussion: 'Is Knowledge probabilistic?' -> No; 'Is the extraction of Knowledge probabilistic?' -> some extraction processes are; 'Is the resulting epistemic state probabilistic?' -> it can be represented probabilistically, but that is regime-dependent; the deeper open question that now emerges is 'What exactly is being represented by the probability?'

a_rows_sample.anchor: What is observed? -> Observation. What makes it evidence? -> Evidence relation. ... What does probability represent? -> Unknown -- investigate. ... Are these actually different lenses on one epistemic state, or are they lenses on different dimensions of it?
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes replacing an immediate 11-framework comparison with a 16-row question/research-target matrix (what is observed->Observation; what makes it evidence->Evidence relation; evidence for what->Proposition/hypothesis; what makes a proposition determined->Determination; what makes determination legitimate->Reasoning/justification; what can be uncertain->Observation/proposition/model/inference; what can be revised->Determination/conclusion/state; what does time change->Validity/evidence/state; what does probability represent->Unknown, investigate; what does logic represent->Inference structure; what does argumentation represent->Support/attack; what does fuzzy value represent->Truth/vagueness; what does D-S represent->Evidence/ignorance; what does epistemic logic represent->Knowledge relation; what does temporal logic represent->Temporal properties; what does measurement theory represent->Empirical-to-numerical representation), then asks whether these are different lenses on one epistemic state or lenses on different dimensions of it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Strong: correctly separates probability from Knowledge; correctly identifies conditional evidence; correctly identifies conditional reasoning; correctly keeps this as research rather than architecture; correctly demands cross-framework comparison. Needs correction: P(F|O) is too simplistic; "established facts" should not automatically be treated as deterministic; the listed common properties are not yet proven invariants; the common algebraic structure is premature; epistemic state may be multidimensional; determination is currently missing as an explicit mathematical object.
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives an explicit verdict on the uploaded framework document: five strong points (correctly separates probability from Knowledge; correctly identifies conditional evidence; correctly identifies conditional reasoning; correctly keeps this as research rather than architecture; correctly demands cross-framework comparison) and six points needing correction (P(F|O) too simplistic; 'established facts' should not automatically be treated as deterministic; listed common properties are not yet proven invariants; the common algebraic structure is premature; epistemic state may be multidimensional; determination is currently missing as an explicit mathematical object). Also explicitly agrees with the framework's constraint: 'Do not design the Kernel. Do not change its boundary. Challenge the architecture; do not become its architect.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: (O, E, F_{<t}, C, R) -> D_t(p) where D_t(p) is the determination of proposition p at time t. Then we investigate how D_t(p) is represented by probability, logic, Dempster-Shafer, argumentation, fuzzy logic, etc. I think that is the next missing piece before we can responsibly talk about the invariant.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes continuing research at exactly one point: formalizing '(O,E,F_{<t},C,R) -> D_t(p)' as the operation producing the determination of proposition p at time t, then investigating how D_t(p) is represented by probability, logic, Dempster-Shafer, argumentation, fuzzy logic, etc. -- framed as the next missing piece before responsibly discussing invariance.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS needs to determine what the organization should currently accept as knowledge, based on incomplete and sometimes conflicting information, and it must be able to explain and revise that determination later. ... Information -> What did we actually observe? -> ... -> What can we defend as "knowledge"?
a_rows_sample.statement: States the business problem in one sentence: KnowledgeOS needs to determine what the organization should currently accept as knowledge, based on incomplete and sometimes conflicting information, and must be able to explain and revise that determination later; there is no direct pipeline from information to knowledge -- it passes through what was observed, what the observation means, what evidence it provides, evidence strength, existing facts/evidence, applicable rules, conflicts, current conclusion, and finally what can be defended as knowledge, with every step conditional and imperfect.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Port 8081 is open. That's an observation. Does it prove Nexus is available? No. It is evidence supporting that possibility. ... another process uses the port; the service is running but inaccessible from the required network; the information is outdated; this is not the production server. So: Observation != Evidence != Fact.
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem 1 (Information is not automatically evidence): 'Port 8081 is open' is an observation, not proof that Nexus is available -- it is evidence supporting that possibility only, since alternative explanations exist (another process on the port, network-inaccessible service, outdated information, wrong server); therefore Observation != Evidence != Fact.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Observation A -> supports "Nexus is running"; Observation B -> supports "Nexus is reachable"; Observation C -> contradicts "Nexus is reachable from production". Now what? We have conflicting evidence. The system must determine: What should we currently conclude? This is the determination problem.
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem 2 (evidence does not automatically create a fact): three observations produce conflicting evidence (A supports 'Nexus is running', B supports 'Nexus is reachable', C contradicts 'Nexus is reachable from production'); the system must determine what to currently conclude -- this is the determination problem.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A system is "migration ready" only if: dependencies are identified; network access is verified; backup is verified; certificates are understood; rollback is defined. ... Dependencies: Strong, Network: Strong, Backup: Uncertain, Certificates: Missing, Rollback: Strong. Can we say "Migration ready"? Not simply by looking at the data. We need the rule for determining readiness.
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem 3 (the rules for determining something matter): given a five-criterion migration-readiness policy (dependencies/network/backup/certificates/rollback) and mixed evidence strength per criterion (Strong/Strong/Uncertain/Missing/Strong), whether 'migration ready' can be asserted cannot be read off the data alone -- an explicit rule for determining readiness is required.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Architect A says: "80% confidence is sufficient. Proceed." Architect B says: "The certificate dependency is unknown. Therefore readiness cannot be established." Both have the same information. But they use different reasoning criteria. ... KnowledgeOS should probably not decide which reasoning system is universally correct. It should preserve enough information so that the appropriate reasoning regime can make its determination.
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem 4 (different reasoning methods can produce different answers): two architects viewing identical evidence reach opposite conclusions (Architect A: '80% confidence is sufficient, proceed' vs Architect B: 'certificate dependency unknown, therefore readiness cannot be established') because they apply different reasoning criteria (Bayesian probability vs logical derivation vs argumentation vs Dempster-Shafer belief+ignorance vs non-monotonic defeasible conclusions); principle derived: KnowledgeOS should probably not decide which reasoning system is universally correct, but should preserve enough information for the appropriate reasoning regime to make its own determination.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We don't yet know what "knowledge" actually is ... Is a highly probable conclusion knowledge? Is a logically derived conclusion knowledge? Is an institutionally approved statement knowledge? Is something knowledge if nobody can explain why it is true? Is an old fact still knowledge after it becomes obsolete? Is "unknown" itself part of knowledge? These are not implementation questions yet. They are domain-definition questions.
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem 6 (we don't yet know what 'knowledge' actually is), the deepest of the six: facts, evidence, observations, justification, reasoning, probability, belief, commitments, conclusions, and knowledge have not yet had their boundaries rigorously established; poses six unresolved domain-definition questions (is a highly probable conclusion knowledge; is a logically derived conclusion knowledge; is an institutionally approved statement knowledge; is something knowledge if nobody can explain why it is true; is an old, obsolete fact still knowledge; is 'unknown' itself part of knowledge) -- explicitly framed as domain-definition questions, not implementation questions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Information -> Evidence -> Reasoning -> Determination -> Knowledge ... contextual; time-dependent; incomplete; sometimes probabilistic; sometimes logical; sometimes argumentative; sometimes governed by explicit rules.
a_rows_sample.statement: Summarizes the business problem as a transformation from Information to Defensible Knowledge via Information->Evidence->Reasoning->Determination->Knowledge, where the transformation is contextual, time-dependent, incomplete, and sometimes probabilistic, logical, argumentative, or governed by explicit rules.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Determination is system-relative. Not Determination(p) but Determination(p\mid\mathcal S,\Gamma) ... This does not mean truth becomes relative. Rather Truth(p) may be fixed while Determination(p|S_1) and Determination(p|S_2) differ.
b_rows_sample.statement: Central correction: Determination(p) should be Determination(p|S,Gamma), varying with formal language/axioms/rules/evidence/context/resources/accessibility, while Truth(p) itself may remain fixed -- truth does not become relative even though what can be determined does.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
three fundamental boundaries: 1. Representation boundary ... 2. Epistemic boundary ... 3. Formal reasoning boundary ... Representation 
eq Evidence 
eq Derivation 
eq Truth ... Unknown 
eq Undecidable 
eq Unprovable 
eq False ... Every determination is relative to an explicit epistemic and reasoning context.
b_rows_sample.statement: Final synthesis converging the three books' contributions (Situation Calculus: Transition/Action/Persistence; Williamson: Knowledge/Evidence/Accessibility/Limits; Godel: FormalSystem/Derivability/MetaLevel/Incompleteness) into a shared dual-pipeline diagram and a three-fundamental-boundaries framing (Representation, Epistemic, Formal-reasoning boundary), yielding the candidate research-constitution principle: 'every determination is relative to an explicit epistemic and reasoning context; inability to derive/decide must not be interpreted as falsity, absence, or absolute unknowability; formal derivability, semantic truth, epistemic standing, and verification are distinct relations requiring explicit bridges'; recommends running KR-GODEL-2026-09 next rather than reading another philosophical book.

a_rows_sample.anchor: whether someone calculates mentally or with pencil and paper can matter to whether the resulting belief counts as knowledge ... EpistemicProcess \not\subseteq InternalState ... epistemic process boundaries cannot be assumed to coincide with the boundary of the agent.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extended-Mind long-division example argues EpistemicProcess is not a subset of InternalState -- process boundaries need not coincide with agent boundaries; for AI systems, a human+retrieval+database+calculator+AI-model+verifier chain may form one epistemic production chain, whose components should be preserved rather than collapsed into a single 'knower'. Explicitly does not mean adopting 'Extended Mind' wholesale.

a_rows_sample.anchor:
social externalism: reliable knowledge can arise from socially distributed cognitive processes ... large scientific collaborations can function as distributed cognitive processes ... EpistemicProcess=IndividualProcess\cup DistributedProcess ... humans are poor at determining sincerity, deception and competence from superficial cues ... Presentation
eq Reliability ... AuthorityCue
eq EvidenceQuality ... Confidence
eq Truth
a_rows_sample.statement: Social externalism (reliable knowledge from socially-distributed cognitive processes, e.g. large scientific collaborations) motivates EpistemicProcess = IndividualProcess ∪ DistributedProcess with a candidate DistributedProcess=(Nodes,Edges,Roles,Transformations,Controls); source-monitoring research (humans poor at judging sincerity/deception/competence from superficial cues) argues Presentation != Reliability, AuthorityCue != EvidenceQuality, Confidence != Truth, and for machine-readable source lineage over reliance on human memory of provenance.

a_rows_sample.anchor: inferentialist non-presumptivism; presumptivism; externalism ... SourceReliability(s,\Gamma) should be conceptually distinct from EvidenceStanding(e). A highly reliable source can provide bad evidence ... SourceReliability\neq EvidenceTruth\neq DeterminationStanding.
a_rows_sample.statement: Compares three testimony theories (favoring externalism) to argue SourceReliability(s,Gamma) must be kept distinct from EvidenceStanding(e) and DeterminationStanding, since a reliable source can give bad evidence on a specific question and an unreliable source can accidentally give true information.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge-that ... Knowledge-wh ... Knowledge-how ... at least some procedural know-how cannot simply be reduced to propositional knowledge. ... K^{that} and K^{how} as research categories ... could become important for the EKS/PKS side of KnowledgeOS.
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates the Ryle-style knowledge-that/knowledge-wh/knowledge-how distinction (procedural know-how not reducible to propositional knowledge), proposing K^that and K^how as research categories relevant to KnowledgeOS's own EKS/PKS (Engineering/Practitioner Knowledge System) side, distinguishing e.g. 'production requires TLS' (knowledge-that) from 'how to safely rotate the certificate' (procedural, embodied in procedure/capability/workflow/skill/executable process).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence \xrightarrow{Basing/Process} Determination \xrightarrow{Evaluation} Standing ... Reliability(Process,Environment,Context) ... Source\rightarrow Acquisition\rightarrow Evidence\rightarrow Process\rightarrow Determination\rightarrow Standing
b_rows_sample.statement: Executive framing: Shieber's most important contribution is a missing middle layer between Evidence and Determination (Basing/Process) and between Determination and Standing (Evaluation), with process reliability relative to environment/context, and a full epistemic-lineage chain Source->Acquisition->Evidence->Process->Determination->Standing; claimed to strengthen Evaluation, Evidence, the succeq ordering, Contr, Zero, Determination, Lifecycle, Provenance, and delta without requiring a Theory v1.2 change.

b_rows_sample.anchor: same apparent evidence + same true conclusion \neq knowledge ... because the process that produced the conclusion is unreliable in that environment [stopped-clock case] ... GoodEvidence(e)\Rightarrow GoodDetermination(d) [rejected]
b_rows_sample.statement: The stopped-clock example (apparently correct evidence + accidentally true conclusion, produced by an unreliable process) is used to reject GoodEvidence(e)=>GoodDetermination(d), motivating the EvidenceQuality/ProcessReliability/Basing decomposition and DeterminationAdequacy=Evidence+Basing+Process+Context as separately inspectable dimensions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: naive foundationalism cannot explain why one perception is reliable and another misleading; externalism can distinguish them by appeal to the reliable accuracy of the perceptual system ... SourceSystem(e)=S ... Source\rightarrow Process\rightarrow Evidence rather than treating Evidence as an atomic thing whose quality is intrinsic.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues evidence quality is not intrinsic but depends on its producing system: proposes a three-level chain Source->Process->Evidence with SourceSystem(e)=S and Reliability(S,Gamma) as the evaluable objects, rather than treating Evidence(e) as atomic.

b_rows_sample.anchor: new evidence is interpreted against what is already known—the prior probability ... does not justify Knowledge = Probability or Confidence = Knowledge. ... b_rows_sample.statement: Bayesian reasoning is used to argue background/prior knowledge affects interpretation of new evidence, Evaluation(e,h,Gamma,K_background), but explicitly does NOT justify Knowledge=Probability or Confidence=Knowledge; Bayesian calculation kept as one candidate evaluation method, not a kernel primitive.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The knowledge-distribution defect ... inject-context.sh injects the entire MEMORY.md and the entire CONTEXT.md ... .claude/MEMORY.md 188,730 bytes ... .claude/CONTEXT.md 954,708 bytes ... injected per session start ≈ 1.14 MB ... the SessionStart hook output was 1.2 MB and was truncated by the consumer
b_rows_sample.statement: First-hand evidence for a knowledge-distribution defect: inject-context.sh injects the ENTIRE MEMORY.md (188,730 bytes) and ENTIRE CONTEXT.md (954,708 bytes) unconditionally, with no selection/scoping/relevance filter/size bound (≈1.14MB per session start, plus the active plan and today's session log); in this very baseline-writing session, the SessionStart hook output (1.2MB) was truncated by its consumer, which persisted it to a file and delivered only a 2KB preview -- 'the knowledge-distribution mechanism exceeded its consumer's ingestion capacity and silently degraded to a pointer.' Strongest possible evidence that the mechanism exists, is active, and does not reliably deliver.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H-KOS-Agent-001: Every knowledge state SHALL be constitutionally coupled to the epistemic agent (Knower) that asserted, observed, or reasoned it. The agent's identity, role, and epistemic capacity are preserved as protected dimensions of the knowledge object.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a first version of the Knower invariant: every knowledge state must be constitutionally coupled to the epistemic agent that produced it, so that 'who knows' remains inseparable from 'what is known'; framed as completing the Tripuṭī (Knower-Knowing-Known) trinity and as the engineering translation of the Gita's Kṣetrajña.

a_rows_sample.anchor: INV-KOS-Agent-001 (Candidate): KnowledgeOS SHALL preserve the epistemic agency associated with every knowledge state, including who observed, who interpreted, who reasoned, who validated, and under which authority context the knowledge state was produced.
a_rows_sample.statement: Refined, 'stronger and more general' successor to H-KOS-Agent-001: preserves epistemic agency (observer/reasoner/validator/authority-context) rather than binding knowledge to a single knower's identity.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ज्ञाता (Jñātā) — Knower | ज्ञान (Jñāna) — Knowing | ज्ञेय (Jñeya) — Known ... Knowledge without epistemic origin loses accountability.
a_rows_sample.statement: Maps the Vedanta Tripuṭī (Jñātā/Jñāna/Jñeya) onto KnowledgeOS interpretation (Epistemic Agent / Reasoning-transformation process / Knowledge object-proposition); the engineering extraction is not metaphysical truth but that knowledge without epistemic origin loses accountability.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Invariant I-11 closes the I-1 hole
a_rows_sample.statement: I-11: no in-force policy -- the AcceptancePolicy and the constitution included -- changes without a governed, versioned approval decision; self-modification of the in-force policy is excluded by construction, not by exhortation. I-11 closes the hole the falsification pass found in I-1: the Knower's ownership now reaches Determination through the governed policy chain instead of stopping short at an unowned policy object.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The Sarathi reading hardens into I-1
a_rows_sample.statement: After the crisis, the corpus reorganized itself around numbered questions -- how does knowledge change state, who owns the goal, what makes evidence sufficient -- and, in parallel, returned to the Gita lens with new seriousness. The era's great gift to the final architecture is the Sarathi (charioteer) reading: the Knower owns the frame; everything else serves it. Of all the era's images, this is the one that hardened into an invariant (I-1) and survived every later regime unchanged. When Part III.2 says the Knower owns problem, purpose, IdealState, and final authority, it is speaking the formalized residue of this reading.
